title: Investment and Financing Constraints: Evidence from the Funding of Corporate Pension Plans
research_question: Do shocks to a firm's internal financial resources causally affect its capital expenditures and other investment outlays (such as R&D and acquisitions), and is this effect concentrated among financially constrained firms? Additionally, do firms not subject to such cash drains absorb investment projects that constrained firms forgo?
data_description: The analysis uses an unbalanced firm-year panel constructed by matching Compustat data on publicly traded U.S. firms to plan-level pension data from IRS Form 5500 filings provided by the Department of Labor. The sample covers fiscal years 1990 to 1998 and contains 8,030 firm-year observations on 1,522 firms that sponsor defined benefit (DB) pension plans with more than 100 participants. Key firm-level variables (scaled by lagged book assets) include capital expenditures, cash flow, non-pension cash flow, Tobin's Q, R&D, acquisitions, dividends, repurchases, debt, trade credit, and working capital. Pension variables include U.S. pension assets, pension liabilities (ABO basis), normal cost, funding status (overfunding minus underfunding), total pension contributions, and constructed mandatory contributions. Auxiliary samples include ~46,848 non-DB Compustat firm-years for general-equilibrium tests and SEC 10-K pension data extending through 2004.
institutional_context: U.S. firms sponsoring defined benefit pension plans must legally fund accrued retirement liabilities in segregated pension trusts. When the market value of plan assets falls below the present value of pledged liabilities, federal law (ERISA, the Pension Protection Act of 1987, and the Retirement Protection Act of 1994) compels the sponsor to make contributions equal to the larger of a minimum funding contribution and a deficit reduction contribution. The required payment is a sharply nonlinear, kinked, and discontinuous function of the plan's funding status: contributions jump to zero once the plan reaches full funding, and the percentage of any shortfall that must be paid in the first year changes abruptly at specific funding thresholds. Annual funding status itself is driven largely by exogenous fluctuations in pension asset returns and in the 30-year Treasury discount rate, which differ across firms because of variation in plan size, benefit structure, and asset allocation. These mandated cash outflows directly reduce internal funds available for corporate investment.
